🕵️ Contradiction – Spot the Liar | 👍 Recommendation: ✅ Yes, with caveats | ⏱ ~6h played

                                                                             - 8,5 / 10 -

=== TL;DR ===

🧠 A surprisingly engaging FMV detective adventure that leans hard into 80s/90s crime-TV nostalgia, memorable (and intentionally exaggerated) performances, and a satisfying contradiction-based investigation system — proof that FMV games still work when done right.

=== What this game is ===

📖 Contradiction – Spot the Liar is a full-motion video (FMV) detective adventure where you assist Inspector Frederick Jenks in solving a suspicious death in a small English village — all within a single night.

What initially looks like a suicide quickly unravels into something far stranger, involving secretive organizations, questionable alibis, and characters who clearly aren’t telling the whole truth. If you enjoy classic crime shows like The X-Files or old-school adventure games, this will feel immediately familiar — and comforting.

=== Gameplay ===

🎮 Core loop: explore locations → interview suspects → collect clues → use dialogue fragments to expose contradictions.

You move between fixed locations using static images (very Myst-like), interview characters, and gather dialogue fragments tied to specific people. Progression depends entirely on catching characters in logical inconsistencies — you know they’re lying, but the challenge is finding exactly where they slipped up.

Player freedom is moderate: you can choose the order of interviews and exploration, but the investigation itself follows a guided structure rather than offering multiple radically different solutions.

=== What it does well ===

✨ Acting & characters: FMV lives or dies by its performances — and Contradiction delivers. The cast leans into deliberate overacting, resulting in memorable, sometimes hilarious characters without breaking the mystery.
🎶 Soundtrack: Tim Follin’s music subtly reinforces tension and discovery without ever becoming intrusive.
🧩 Contradiction system: Catching a lie by piecing together someone’s own words is genuinely satisfying and remains the game’s strongest mechanic.

=== Where it falls short ===

⚠ Late-game UI friction: As your list of dialogue fragments grows, finding a specific remembered contradiction can become cumbersome.
⚠ Style won’t be for everyone: The exaggerated acting, FMV format, and self-aware absurdity may turn off players expecting modern, subdued storytelling.

=== Replayability ===

🔁 Low. Outside of revisiting the story for nostalgia or achievements, the experience shines most on a first playthrough.

=== Who should play ===

✅ Fans of FMV games and classic adventure titles
✅ Players who enjoy detective stories and logical deduction
✅ Anyone nostalgic for 80s/90s TV vibes (X-Files, A-Team, Command & Conquer energy)

🚫 Players who dislike FMV or exaggerated performances
🚫 Those looking for deep mechanical systems or modern cinematic realism

=== Technical & value ===

🛠 Performance: Smooth and stable; no crashes or major issues encountered.
🎮 Controls/UI: Simple and intuitive, though late-game clue management could be improved.
💰 Length: ~5–8 hours (perfect for a rainy Sunday). Worth the price, especially for genre fans.

=== Final verdict ===

🏁 Contradiction – Spot the Liar tells a compelling detective story with charm, confidence, and a clear love for classic FMV adventures. It doesn’t modernize away its roots — it embraces them fully. FMV games aren’t dead — they just need to be designed right. This one is.

Contradiction is almost like a strange relic. It's a fully FMV point-and-click adventure built around a crime story, but it's also a weird budget game that relies on a bit of narm charm to get by. 

We follow Inspector Jenks as he investigates the mysterious death of Kate Vine, a student in a sleepy English village. Technically already ruled a suicide, Jenks is nonetheless unconvinced as the details don't add up and it feels like everyone in her life, from her friends to the local pub landlady and the shifty business school Atlas that she attended, have things to hide. 

Gameplay is strictly point-and-click as you navigate Jenks around the town and into interrogations with the locals. The main way you progress is by finding parts of each person's statements that, as the name says, contradict - if you've played Ace Attorney it's a tiny bit like that. 

Unfortunately there are some problems that mar the experience. Firstly is that sometimes the correct statements simply don't seem to contradict and require you to make an additional connecting leap in your mind. It also feels a lot like the writers didn't start with a strong spine for the plot - elements get introduced or fall out from focus at random, and the story pulls in a ton of different directions by the endgame, with no satisfying resolutions for many of them. It's a shame; there's still a weird early-90s charm to this that I want to love.

This game gets a ton of slack because it's such an interesting project and we're starved for modern FMV and investigation games.  The story is engaging, the characters are interesting, and the acting is charming.  

However, to say the ending is "a disappointment" is an understatement.  It's unbelievably dissatisfying.  Most of the mysteries you've been unraveling have absolutely no meaning.  By the end, your notebook is filled with several plot lines that have zero impact on the ending and get no conclusion.  You randomly point out a mundane contradiction and the killer confesses for no reason.  

The gameplay is often frustrating.  The interface is terrible and confusing.  Notes quickly become disorganized and overwhelming.  There's a TON of pointless backtracking.  Talk to one person, get a clue, then travel around and ask everyone about the clue.  Even with fast travel, you need several clicks and short ~2 second cutscenes (that you've seen dozens of times) to talk to someone.  It's like a walking simulator to slow down the pace of the game and stretch the playtime.   

The main gameplay element is finding contradictions, but they're mostly stupid easy.  You never cross-reference people's stories, so it's literally just calling a character out for saying one thing ("I'm allergic to ___") and then saying the opposite later ("Yes I took a pill of ____").  The contradictions only FEEL hard because tracking information is so difficult that you can't put the pieces together without slogging through your evidence bag. 

Also, final rant point, you can't change the volume.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 18:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️/10

I didn’t expect to enjoy this game as much as I did. It’s an FMV detective story from a bygone era—complete with awkward zoom-ins, stiff body language, and a main character who looks permanently bewildered. But somehow? It works. Like, really works.

There’s something weirdly charming and compelling about poking holes in lies with just the right contradiction, watching suspects flail as you pin them down with their own words. It’s part detective sim, part campy stage play, and somehow greater than the sum of its very strange parts. It’s janky. It’s dated. And it’s at memorable mystery game!

🕰️ [b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Surprisingly great acting and voice direction (Jenks is a gem)
[*]  The contradiction mechanic is so satisfying when it clicks
[*]  Genuinely fun to play detective and uncover lies
[*]  Weird little village setting adds to the cozy, eerie atmosphere
[*]  Still runs well on modern machines, including Mac
[*]  Memorable characters, from creepy cultists to awkward teens
[/list]
❌ Cons:
[list]
[*] No real replay value once you've solved it
[*] Bit short (~7-8 hours to 100%)
[*]  UI is a little clunky by today’s standards
[*]  Pacing can drag if you miss a contradiction and get stuck
[/list]
